extracted.intended_audience: aspiring fiction writers seeking publication (short stories and novels)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance on preparing, formatting, pitching, and submitting short stories and novels to magazines, agents, and publishers, including how to choose markets and evaluate agents. Emphasizes completion, quality control, and professional presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completed manuscript requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: You must have a completed piece of writing — not an idea or a few pages, but a fully finished work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beginning, middle, and end: the whole thing. No one will sell or represent an idea alone; you have to write the book/story yourself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finish first draft and multiple revisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Start a project and finish the first draft; if serious, take it through numerous drafts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete at least a short story (use an exercise as a springboard if needed). Finishing is the most important step; revision and polishing follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality control / make the product outstanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure that your novel, novella, or short story is outstandingly good before submitting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and agents are busy and will not discern hidden merit; rigorous self-editing or external critique is required. Consider hiring a manuscript analyst to identify and fix weaknesses and to assess market potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of manuscript analysts / freelance editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscript analysts (freelance editors, professional readers, book doctors) can identify what's wrong and how to fix it, and evaluate market potential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check credentials; prefer published authors or industry-experienced people. Ask for references and sample reports. Good analysts provide industry-level criticism and increase chances of acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard manuscript formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow standard formatting to make a professional impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use black type on white 8.5-by-11-inch paper; choose a 12-point font (preferably Times New Roman, Courier, Courier New, or Arial); indent paragraphs; double-space; one-inch margins all around; number pages in the upper right-hand corner; spell-check and proofread by a human; include a title page with title, word count, your name, address, phone number, and e-mail (also put this info on the first manuscript page); keep pages loose-leaf.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting absolute no-no's
rubrics_metrics.description: Things that will mark you as amateur and should be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use fancy graphics or typesetting; do not staple or bind pages; avoid gimmicky devices unless they are exceptionally apt and witty; do not include head shots, photos of kids or pets, or pencil drawings with your submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include SASE with postal submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Always include a stamped self-addressed envelope (SASE) when sending anything by post to an agent or editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a large SASE if you want the manuscript back; use a small one for a reply only and specify in your letter that the manuscript need not be returned. No SASE, no response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright basics for manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright protection is automatic when you put words to paper, but registration has advantages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You cannot copyright an idea (premise), but you can protect the execution. Registration with the U.S. Copyright Office allows you to file an infringement action. Do not call attention to copyright on your query or manuscript — it looks amateur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Query letter core components
rubrics_metrics.description: A query letter (cover letter) should pique an agent's or editor's interest and demonstrate your writing ability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include an opening line(s) introducing your story/novel and why you're contacting that particular agent/editor; a brief pitch showcasing character and situation (book-jacket style: intrigue, don't explain); a bit about you (relevant credits or expertise, but don't oversell); and a closing stating you've enclosed an SASE and that you look forward to a response. Salutation must include the agent/editor's name. Be professional, concise, and let your voice show.

rubrics_metrics.name: Query pitch length and style
rubrics_metrics.description: Tailor the pitch within the query to the form: short stories vs novels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For short stories, a line or two is sufficient. For novels, one well-crafted paragraph. Pretend you're writing book-jacket copy—intrigue rather than explain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate you've read the target market
rubrics_metrics.description: Show in your query that you know the magazine/agent's work and why your submission fits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mention specific reasons (e.g., the agent represents a similar writer, or the magazine publishes fiction with a strong narrative line). Saying you've bought and read an issue can help; editors appreciate evidence you've studied the market.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting literary magazines (market fit analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose magazines whose published fiction corresponds to your work in content and style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult market guides, buy/read copies, analyze subject matter, tone, syntax, POV, setting, language, and narrative focus. Read at least three different litmags to find those that feel right for your work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use market guides to find markets and agents
rubrics_metrics.description: Consult authoritative market directories and periodicals to find publishers, magazines, and agents and learn submission specs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended guides include Writer's Market; Novel and Short Story Writer's Market; The International Directory of Little Magazines and Small Presses; CLMP Directory; Poets & Writers magazine; The Writer magazine. Verify contact names by phone/email.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short stories: submit directly to magazines (no agent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally do not use an agent for individual short stories; submit to magazines yourself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agents rarely handle individual short story submissions because the profit is meager. Target litmags and glossies directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the slush pile and initial screening
rubrics_metrics.description: Most unsolicited submissions end up in the slush pile and are screened by assistants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many submissions are poorly written or incorrectly formatted. Editorial assistants know what to look for; professional presentation and rigorous quality control increase odds of surviving initial screening.

rubrics_metrics.name: What agents do for authors
rubrics_metrics.description: An agent's fundamental role is to sell your work and handle related professional tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agents read and suggest revisions; submit to appropriate editors; negotiate terms; exploit additional rights (foreign, serial, film); examine contract clauses; track payments; and may help with promotion or grievance resolution. Agents typically take 10–15% commission.

rubrics_metrics.name: What agents look for in a writer/work
rubrics_metrics.description: Agents seek originality and a work they can be passionate about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for a singular literary voice, a new perspective on the human condition, a view of a place we've not seen before, or strong elements like humor. The ideal client inspires genuine passion — trust and a shared vision are critical in the agent-author relationship.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to research and identify suitable agents
rubrics_metrics.description: Find agents who represent writers similar to you and research their client lists and tastes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check acknowledgments in novels to find agents, search the internet, review publisher press releases and catalogs, and read Publisher's Weekly 'Hot Deals' to see who's selling what. Use agent directories but confirm details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow each agent's submission specifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Send exactly what each agent requests (query only, query + synopsis, or sample pages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most agents do not want the whole novel initially. Read agent entries in reference books and follow their requested format to the letter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative submission strategy: send ~50 pages
rubrics_metrics.description: Some authors choose to send a query plus about fifty pages to demonstrate they can shape a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fifty pages can show structure and story-shaping ability where first novels are episodic. A synopsis may cause loss of interest; hooking the reader on the first page is often preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage simultaneous submissions and initial agent list size
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with a small set of agents rather than querying all found names at once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with three or four agents to learn from responses and preserve opportunities. Some agents have no-multiple-submission policies; respect exclusivity requests. Respond quickly when an agent requests more material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Response etiquette and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow agents/editors reasonable time to reply and follow up politely if needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an agent requests the entire manuscript, send it promptly. Allow eight weeks for a response; a polite follow-up is permissible after that. Don't pester by email/phone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing among multiple agent offers
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate agent fit by meeting/talking and assessing shared vision and trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange meetings/extended conversations; decide swiftly once you've selected an agent; send polite thank-you notes to others to preserve relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of nonlegitimate agents and scams
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid agents who solicit manuscripts via classified ads or who charge reading fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Red flags include 'established agent accepting manuscripts' ads and requests for money/reading fees or referrals to expensive 'editors' (kickbacks). Legitimate agents make money from sales, not author fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify agent legitimacy and ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Confirm an agent's credentials and track record before signing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check membership in the Association of Authors' Representatives (AAR) as one indicator (members meet professional standards and don't charge reading fees). Interview the agent, ask for recent sales, and investigate their track record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of responses and how to react
rubrics_metrics.description: Know the common kinds of replies you'll receive and appropriate reactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No response: let it go. Form rejection: common, not necessarily a reflection on quality. Personalized rejection: encouraging sign if they give specific feedback. Rejection with invitation to resubmit: encouraging; incorporate recommended changes. Acceptance: celebrate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical exercises to build readiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform tasks recommended by the book to develop submission readiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises include finishing a short story, writing a query letter, selecting target magazines, and compiling a list of suitable agents to motivate completion and submission.
